summary: The narrator, a young San Francisco student involved with the Xnet movement, reflects after a press conference that he felt proud of, only to find the press portrayed the group as terrorists or terrorist dupes. A Fox News commentator coined the insult "Cal-Quaeda," anti-war leaders disowned the group, and the DHS announced doubled security, staged a demonstration of an arphid cloner, and began arresting alleged Xnet "ringleaders." The narrator, who is suspended from school, avoids blogging about the coverage, keeps working on his papers, and is frisked several times a day, but he is not arrested.
one_line: A San Francisco student's pride in his Xnet press conference turns to dread as the press and DHS brand the movement as terrorists.
key_facts: The narrator rode home after a press conference and thought about Ange, his mother smiling at him, and the press-conference itself.
The narrator's mom was waiting up for him and asked about the movie, and he gave a response he had worked out in advance, cribbing from a review in the Bay Guardian.
The narrator felt proud of the press conference because big-shot journalists showed up and listened to him and people who shared his beliefs.
The press concluded that the Xnet group were terrorists or terrorist dupes after the press conference.
A Fox News reporter devoted a ten-minute commentary to the group, talking about their "criminal treason."
The Fox News reporter proposed calling the group "Cal-Quaeda" and said they do the terrorists' work on the home front.
One anti-war movement leader went on TV to say he believed the group had been fabricated by the DHS to discredit the anti-war movement.
The DHS announced at a press conference that it would double security in San Francisco.
The DHS demonstrated an arphid cloner in action by using it to stage a car-theft.
The DHS warned people to be alert for young people behaving suspiciously, especially those whose hands were out of sight.
The narrator finished a paper on Kerouac and started a paper about the Summer of Love, when the anti-war movement and the hippies converged on San Francisco in 1967.
By the end of the week, the narrator was frisked an average of four times a day.
The narrator was suspended, and a police officer eyeballed a letter from Chavez saying so.
Every night the DHS announced more arrests of alleged Xnet "ringleaders" and "operatives" who were paraded on TV with arphid sniffers and other devices.
